content:
As in the title.

Context: I was looking at #mathlib4 > Duplication of code between typeclass and structure? and thought that for a type S, if one has an instance SubgroupClass S G, then for every s : S, s is a subgroup, whose elements are elements of G. But the code doesn't guarantee G is a group (only a DivInvMonoid), and it doesn't check inv_mul_cancel in S either.

Perhaps I was unclear. What I mean is: with the current definition of SubgroupClass, I can define type A and T, object H : A, such that

example [DivInvMonoid T] [SubgroupClass A T] :
  ∃ (a : T), a ∈ H ∧ a⁻¹ * a ≠ 1

compiles.

One would expect SubgroupClass A T to say that every object of type A is a group of elements of type T, but the above shows it isn't.

It's true when T is a group! But less cheekily, indeed, we sometimes fib slightly in favor of using more familiar names, because what mathematician (or formalization expert for that matter) wants to read DivInvMonoidClass?

docs#DivInvMonoid is the sort of thing that only exists because there happen to be just enough use cases in practice that it saves some code duplication, and so we keep it around despite the fact that it doesn't correspond to any algebraic structure that mathematicians use day-to-day. So the fact that it exhibits oddities with regards to SubgroupClass is maybe not so suprising, and we don't mind.

user202729 said:

compiles.

Presumably, you don't mean that this compiles, but rather that you have a proof of this?

I will note that this is further support for my concept that these classes are, functionally, abstractions of membership closure rules and not abstractions of concrete subjects. There is no use for "the terms of this type represent sets forming subgroups" as opposed to "the terms of this type represent sets closed under identity, multiplication and inversion." In the first case, you should just write down a map from your type to Subgroup G!
